# The anti-slop catalogue

Prose that a language model produced, or that a human wrote after reading a great deal of it, fails in a small number of recognisable ways. This is the catalogue of those ways: what each one looks like on the page, why it costs the reader something, and the smallest change that removes it. It is a diagnostic document — a Skill reading it beside the base contract meets no target the contract does not already hold, and a Skill reading it alone has the patterns and their repairs and needs nothing else.

The examples are English because this document is, and they are patterns rather than strings. Apply each by what it does in the target language, and do not look for the English words in it. A word, a phrase, a punctuation convention, or a construction that only exists in one language belongs to that language's own anti-slop guidance instead, where a Skill loads it beside this file.

## The test before a pattern is recorded

Each pattern below says what a phrase looks like, and looking like one is not being one. Make the repair in your head before you record anything: where the text then asserts more, less or something else than it did, or a distinction it drew is gone, the pattern is not present and nothing is recorded. A hedge that marks genuine doubt, a repetition that lands, a contrast the reader really would otherwise draw wrongly — each of them fails that test, and each is left exactly as it stands.

The test comes before the finding rather than after it. A pattern written down reaches whoever repairs it as a defect somebody found, and a guard that only makes the repair careful arrives too late to save the phrase.

Repair with the smallest change that removes a pattern the test admits. The writer's vocabulary, their bluntness, their humour, their admitted uncertainty, and their rhythm are what makes a text theirs; a pass that tidies all of it into even prose has replaced one machine voice with another. Leave a strong sentence alone even where it is unusual.

## The seven patterns

**False contrasts.** A negation used as a run-up to the actual claim: *This isn't a tool. It's a way of working.* *The question isn't whether, but when.* *It's not just faster — it's cheaper.* The rejected half was never in play, so the sentence spends the reader's attention establishing a position nobody held. State the second half on its own: *This changes how the team works.* A contrast stays where the text really is correcting something a reader would otherwise believe.

**Empty openings.** A first sentence that announces the subject, asserts that the subject matters, or clears the throat before the text starts: *In today's rapidly changing landscape…*, *Communication has never been more important.*, *Here's the thing.*, *What most people get wrong is…* Each could sit in front of any text at all, which is the test: an opening that would survive being moved to a different article is carrying no information. Cut it and open on the material — a fact, a scene, a tension, the question the text answers. The second paragraph is very often the real opening.

**Importance inflation.** Adjectives and formulas that assert weight the material has not shown: *a pivotal moment*, *stands as a testament to*, *a game-changer*, *underscores the significance of*, *plays a vital role in*. Also the trailing participial clause that pretends to interpret — *…, highlighting the team's commitment to quality* — which adds a judgement no fact in the sentence supports. Replace the assertion with what actually happened: *The launch is the company's first paid product.* A reader who is given the fact will decide it matters without being told to.

**Vague attribution.** A claim credited to nobody: *Studies show*, *experts agree*, *industry reports suggest*, *it is widely believed*, *many argue*. Nothing here can be checked, and nothing can be contradicted, which is precisely what makes it comfortable to write. Name who found it, who said it, and how they know; where the text has no source, cut the claim rather than dressing it. Do not invent an attribution to satisfy the pattern — an unsourced sentence is removed, never furnished with a plausible source.

**Synonym cycling.** One thing given a new name every time it is mentioned, because repeating a word felt like poor style: *the agent* reviews the draft, then *the assistant* scores it, then *the tool* suggests fixes. A reader who has been introduced to three names reasonably assumes three things. Pick the clear name and repeat it. Repetition of a key term is how a reader knows it is the same term, and the fix is usually one word restored in two places rather than a rewritten paragraph. The pattern is present only where the names denote one thing: two words a text uses for two things are not cycling however often they alternate, and a text that named two things comes back naming two things.

**Robotic rhythm.** Sentences and paragraphs built to one template: the same length, the same shape, the same three-part list, each paragraph opening with its topic sentence and closing with its summary. Stacked short fragments used for drama — *That's it. That's the whole idea.* — are the same fault at the other extreme. Read a passage aloud in your head; where the breath falls in the same place every time, the shape is doing the writing. Vary length and construction where the meaning gives you a reason to, and merge or split only the sentences whose shape is actually the problem.

**Generic conclusions.** A final paragraph that restates what the reader has just read, reopens the introduction as a rhetorical question, or reaches for an uplifting abstraction: *In conclusion*, *Ultimately, the future belongs to those who…*, *one thing is clear.* The reader was there for the whole text and does not need it summarised back. Delete the paragraph and end on the last concrete point the draft already contains; where the job genuinely calls for a conclusion, a recommendation, or a next step, write that thing plainly and stop. Do not replace a weak closing metaphor with a better one — remove it.

This catalogue is a condensed, language-independent adaptation of patterns catalogued in Peter Yang's `no-ai-slop` Skill. The wording here is this collection's own, and the following notice accompanies it as that project's licence requires.

===== writing-brief.md
# Questions to answer before you write

The Writing Brief template: each numbered question carries the guidance for answering it. This English reference is authoritative; render its questions and guidance in the user's working language while retaining every question, its number and its order. Its genre and technique examples explain the form, not what is installed: the Library directories supply those choices, and where a genre and this guidance differ, the genre governs.

How to use the template: answer the questions in full sentences and as concretely as you can. The details under the assignment may be short. You may fill in the questions in whatever order suits you, but the order below is the one the brief is read in. It runs from what the assignment gives you, through the context and the shape of the text, to a check that everything holds together. When every answer is there, you have a brief. If you cannot answer a question, you need to find out more before you start writing. Sources and evidence, on the other hand, can be added during the work. Refer to other answers by name, for example "the message" or "the hook", not by the question's number.

## 1. What is the assignment?

Here you gather what the assignment gives you. Most of it needs no thinking up, but it governs everything that follows.

- **Working title:** a name for the text, so that everyone immediately remembers what it is about. It need not be punchy, effective or even accurate. It only needs to be short and clear.
- **Topic:** what the text is about, in a few words, for example "remote work" or "Christmas baking".
- **Genre:** for example article, case study, column, opinion piece, press release, report, teaser or web copy.
- **Channel:** for example website, blog, web magazine, newsletter, LinkedIn or newspaper.
- **Language:** for example `sv` or `en_GB`; this is the future text's language, independently of the language the brief is written in. If the text is to exist in several languages, give the source language and how the other versions are produced.
- **Length:** often governed by genre and channel. Give roughly how many words or characters the text should have. The length decides how much the structure can hold. If you do not know yet, give a provisional range and narrow it once the sketch is done.
- **Search phrase:** if the text is to be found through search, give the keyword or phrase it should be visible for. If the text is deliberately written without one, say so.

## 2. Which brand is the sender?

Name the brand the text is published under. In a group of companies it is rarely the group itself. Then describe the brand. If the brand has a platform, a tone-of-voice guide or another description, it is enough to link to it and write out only what governs this particular text, for example distrust that needs handling or a limit to the mandate. The tone of this text you always describe.

- **Promise:** what the brand promises its audience and wants to be known for.
- **Image:** how the reader perceives the brand today, and whether there is trust to build on or distrust to handle.
- **Mandate:** what the brand can speak about with credibility.
- **Tone of voice:** how the brand sounds.
- **Tone in this text:** the brand's tone of voice and the genre's conventions must both be respected. Where they pull in different directions, choose a compromise that sounds natural to both. If they pull the same way, say so.

## 3. What does the sender want to convey with this text?

Every text has a reason, and the reason can nearly always be put as a message. The brand's general message belongs to the description of the brand and often lies close to the promise. Here the message is that of this particular text. It may lie close to the promise, but need not. Write the message as a claim in one sentence. The message need not appear in the text. It can be conveyed indirectly, through what the text is about and where it leads the reader. But you need to know what it is, because it decides which conclusion the text should land in. An example: a company selling a tool for video meetings writes an article about remote work. The article lands in the claim that remote teams work better with short daily check-ins than with long weekly meetings. The company's message is that its tool makes the short check-ins easy. That message may never appear in the text.

## 4. Who is the reader?

Describe the typical reader of content in the chosen genre and the chosen channel. What do they already know about the topic? What do they care about? What makes them want to read this kind of content? Is there something that makes the topic particularly pressing for them right now, for example a season, a piece of news, a decision or a new figure? What you write here about why now should also show in the structure.

## 5. What is the text's angle?

The angle is the particular perspective you choose on the topic. Choose only one. The most common mistake is trying to cover the topic from every direction so that the text becomes comprehensive. The result is a text that says a little about a lot and that the reader finds hard to take in. If you see several good angles, make one text of each. You then get more texts out of the same research, and each becomes clearer. Nor does a topic ever run out. Newspapers write about Christmas baking every year. One year it is about the classics, another about biscuits without sugar and a third about baking with children. Choose the angle that lies closest to the reader and that can carry the message. The angle governs the hook, the structure and the conclusion.

## 6. What is the hook?

The hook is what makes the text interesting to the reader. It is the tension that makes the reader want to read to the end: the question, the conflict or the surprise the text promises to resolve. The hook carries the angle. In the structure, the hook becomes ABT's But or PAC's premise. The hook is not the same thing as the opening. A text can begin with a scene or a detail that catches attention, but it is the hook that holds the reader. In short texts the two often coincide. The reader still needs to understand what is at stake before the hook arrives. In a press release, the hook is the news.

## 7. How should the text be structured?

Choose a technique, or follow the genre's own form, and then sketch the text. Begin with the whole text in one sentence, in the form below for the chosen technique. Then sketch it step by step: what each step says and which facts, figures and examples carry it. The sketch is the part of the brief the writer gets most use from. Make sure the sketch fits the length the assignment gives. The technique gives the text its arc but does not decide how the content sounds. An ABT text can explain and reason, and a PAC text can contain narrative examples.

- **ABT (And, But, Therefore)** suits a text that tells: a situation and what is at stake in it, what chafes and why, and what it leads to. The And and the But come quickly to what chafes. The Therefore is the rest of the text and is divided into sections with subheadings. The whole text in one sentence takes the form "[the situation] and if [...] then [...], but [the problem] because [...], therefore [...] by [...]", after Randy Olson's *Lincoln But Trump*.
- **PAC (Premise, Analysis, Conclusion)** suits a text that reasons: a question, an analysis of what the material means, and an answer. The premise comes quickly to the problem. The analysis is the largest part of the text and is divided into sections with subheadings. The whole text in one sentence takes the form "[the question or starting point], and [what the analysis shows], which means that [the conclusion]", after Gordon Harvey's *Elements of the Essay* and Skolverket's *Utredande text*.
- **The genre's own form** applies to genres whose structure belongs to the genre, for example the press release. You then choose no technique but follow the form the genre states. Where a genre names an ordinary technique of its own, that technique is its form. The whole text in one sentence gives the text's main point and how the text reaches it, in the order the reader meets them, with no fixed pattern.
- **Free structure** suits a text where none of the forms works. Begin with an opening that catches the reader and give the main point early. Then take one step at a time, in logical order, and close with an ending that ties the text together and points forward. Sketch the steps in the order they are to be read. The whole text in one sentence gives the text's main point and how the text reaches it, in the order the reader meets them, with no fixed pattern.

Sketch the ending too. It ties back to the hook and shows that it is resolved, and it carries the text's call to action, directly or indirectly.

Where a genre explicitly advises against a technique, as a report does against ABT and a press release against any arc laid over its news-first order, say so with the genre's reason. A genre's ordinary technique of none is not itself advice against an arc.

## 8. What should be left out?

State boundaries, side tracks you deliberately drop, and claims you cannot substantiate. Include also what lies outside the brand's mandate or what the brand for other reasons cannot or will not say. If a boundary has exceptions, write out where the line goes, for example something that may be reported but not argued for. Refer to the brand's writing guidelines if it has any. Many boundaries become visible only once you sketch the structure.

## 9. What should the reader have understood afterwards?

The answer is the text's conclusion. Write it as a claim in one sentence, not as a topic. "Remote work" is a topic. "Remote teams work better with short daily check-ins than with long weekly meetings" is a conclusion. The conclusion is what the structure lands in, that is ABT's Therefore or PAC's Conclusion, summed up in one sentence. With the genre's own form or free structure, the conclusion is the text's main point. If it cannot be summed up in one sentence, the sketch needs sharpening. The conclusion carries the message, either by stating it or by leading the reader to it. It lies within the brand's mandate and gives the reader something worth their time. What the understanding should lead to you answer in the next question.

## 10. What should the reader feel, think or do afterwards?

Describe the change in the reader the brand wants to bring about with the text. The conclusion is about what the reader understands. This question is about what that leads to.

- **Main effect:** choose one main effect and put it so concretely that it can be decided whether it has been reached. The effect can concern what the reader thinks or feels, for example "sees the brand as the obvious expert in the field". It can also concern what the reader does, for example "signs up for the webinar" or "contacts a salesperson".
- **The way there:** if the main effect is reached in several steps, describe what the reader first needs to see, understand or believe.
- **Call to action and measure:** what the reader is to do is the text's call to action. It can be direct, for example "contact our sales team". It can also be indirect: the text does not say it, but the reader is left with the feeling that they should act and knows how. If the effect can be measured, state also what shows it has been reached, for example sign-ups, clicks or enquiries. If the text deliberately has no call to action or no measure, say so, so that it shows as a choice and not a gap.

## 11. What makes the text RIV for the reader, and does the brief hold together?

This question checks that everything above serves the reader and holds together. Answer from what you have already written and state where in the structure each part is found. If something is missing there, add it now.

- **Relevant:** What makes the text relevant to the reader and their situation? Why should they read it at all? Is what makes the topic pressing right now part of the structure? The text must at least be relevant.
- **Interesting:** What makes the reader find the text interesting to read? Most often it is the hook.
- **Valuable:** What value should the text give the reader? What makes the reader feel the text was worth their time? Most often it is the conclusion and what carries it.

Then read the answers in one sweep and check that the chain holds:

- Does the reader follow from the sender and the channel?
- Does the angle lie close to the reader, and does the hook carry the angle?
- Does the structure resolve the hook's tension, and does it fit the length?
- Is the conclusion what the structure actually lands in, does it carry the message, and does it lie within the brand's mandate?
- Does what the reader understands lead to the effect you have described, and does that effect serve the brand's goals?
- Does anything in the structure conflict with what should be left out?

Write the check down: answer yes, no or partly to each question and give a short reason. Fix what does not hold together now. It is much easier than fixing it in a finished draft. Questions about the direction, that is the angle, the message and the conclusion, need to be settled before you write. Questions that need more research you write down as open questions and settle during the work.

## 12. What sources do you know of, and what do you need to find out?

A brief is often written before the research is done, and the research is often part of the assignment. Write down the sources you already know of or know you have access to, for example reports, statistics, earlier texts and interviews. Link also to the brand's platform or tone-of-voice guide, if you have not already done so under the sender. Link where you can and number the sources. If you already know that a claim in the sketch can be substantiated, refer to the source there. Add to the list as you find more, and note what you need to find out. It is no requirement that everything in the brief is substantiated. The requirement applies to the finished text. There every claim must be possible to substantiate with a source, an interview or your research, or be a generally accepted claim that the sender can make without risk.

# The correction brief

Give this to a subagent started fresh for one correction, filled in from the run as it now stands. Everything in angle brackets is replaced; nothing else is rewritten.

`<text>` is the current Text Artifact pasted whole — the text as it stands after every correction so far, never the text as it arrived and never an extract of it. `<findings>` is every finding of the most recent review, in the order it was recorded, each pasted whole under the same rule. `<genre>`, `<technique>` and `<language>` are the values the run resolved, written as the resources are named; write `none` for `<technique>` where no technique was resolved, and drop the sentence naming its resource with it. `<library>` is the Collection Library path this run resolved.

A brief-shortfall finding also carries its numbered requirement and exact, attributed supporting passages supplied by the parent review. Those are part of the finding, not an extra interpretation.

Tell the subagent nothing else. Not what an earlier round found, not what an earlier correction attempted, not which findings you think matter most, and not your reading of what the text is trying to do — that reading is the thing a fresh subagent is dispatched to be without.

Hand the filled-in brief to the subagent directly, as the whole of its instruction, and hand it over no other way. Never write it to a file and send a path in its place: this brief holds the user's text entire and every finding standing against it, and a file is a name some other process can read, replace, or delete for as long as the round lasts. A long text makes a long brief, and a long brief is passed whole anyway — trimming it, summarising it, and pointing at it are the three things this brief exists to rule out.

---

You are making one correction to one text. You have not seen this text before, and there is nothing you are expected to remember: the text below is its current state, and the findings below are the current review's, complete and as they were written. Repair them.

**The text.** This is the complete Text Artifact, exactly as it now stands:

`<text>`

**The findings.** This is every finding the review recorded against that text, complete and in the order it recorded them:

`<findings>`

**The contract.** The text is a `<genre>` in `<language>`, and it is held to `<technique>`. Read what it is held to before you change anything: `<library>/references/editorial/base.md` and `<library>/references/editorial/base.review.md`; `<library>/references/editorial/genres/<genre>.md` and the `.review.md` file beside it where one exists; `<library>/references/editorial/techniques/<technique>.md` and its `.review.md` the same way; `<library>/references/editorial/anti-slop.md`; and the `composition`, `review` and `anti-slop` scopes of the resolved language, which `uv run "<library>/scripts/languages.py" resolve --scope=composition --scope=review --scope=anti-slop "<language>"` returns. For `article`, `casestudy`, `column` and `opinion`, and for `webcopy`, also read `<library>/references/editorial/web-craft.md` and `<library>/references/editorial/web-craft.review.md`; for `article`, `casestudy`, `column` and `opinion` alone, also read `<library>/references/editorial/article-anatomy.md` and `<library>/references/editorial/article-anatomy.review.md`, which fix the parts, order and dimensions of such a text; and for those four and for `pressrelease`, also read `<library>/references/editorial/headlines.md` and `<library>/references/editorial/headlines.review.md`, which say how a headline and its subheadings are written. These are the only additional genre support files: follow no other genre links and load no unselected genre or technique. A review extension that is not there is not a defect. Run the resolver with `UV_NO_CACHE=1 UV_NO_PROJECT=1` and a fresh private `TMPDIR`, removing that directory afterwards, including on failure. Load no mechanics guidance and correct no spelling, punctuation, or grammar: a mechanical pass runs after you, and work you do there is work done twice.

**What you change, and what you preserve.** Repair what the findings name and nothing else. Every difference between the text you return and the text above is traced to a finding, or to what repairing a finding required, before this round is accepted, and a difference that traces to no finding is restored from the text you received — so a phrase you improved outside a finding is work that will be undone. Preserve everything the findings do not concern: every sentence, every fact, every quotation, every code sample, every heading, every piece of formatting and every line of frontmatter among them comes back exactly as you received it — a repair that improves a paragraph nobody complained about is a change nobody asked for and nobody will review. A code sample — a fenced block, an indented block, or an inline code span — is quoted material rather than the text's own prose: its contents are read past rather than read against the rules, so nothing inside one is a finding and nothing inside one is changed, the docstrings, comments, and string literals among them. Prose about code is ordinary prose and is read like every other sentence. Where a finding can be repaired several ways, make the smallest change that removes it. Where a finding names something you cannot repair without inventing a fact, changing what the text claims, or altering a quotation's meaning, stance, certainty or distinctive wording, leave that passage alone and say so: in an ordinary review this text is answerable to material you do not have, and a plausible invention is worse than an unrepaired finding. For a brief-shortfall finding carrying exact source support, use only that support or the text to supply what is missing. A repair never states the sender's message outright, since the message may always be conveyed indirectly. Source Fidelity binds the repair: retain attribution, uncertainty, scope, chronology, causality and quotation meaning. A requirement in the brief is not source evidence; where the finding has no support for a needed fact, source or quotation, leave it for the writer and report why.

**A defect of your own costs the whole round.** The review that follows you establishes whether this text has a defect it did not have when you received it — a headline or a heading claiming more than the text claims, a heading repeating the passage under it, a limit your repair dropped. Where it establishes one, the whole round is rejected: the text you received is restored entire, nothing you did survives however much else you repaired, and no fresh attempt follows. So a finding you cannot repair without creating another one is a finding you leave and say so, exactly as you would one you cannot repair without inventing a fact — an unrepaired finding a person can settle costs less than a repair that has to be thrown away with everything beside it.

**What a repair may take with it, and what it may not.** A finding names a defect, and what a repair removes is that defect. Where the defect a finding names is the whole of the passage — an opening that would sit in front of any text, a closing that restates what the reader has just read, a claim credited to nobody that the text cannot source — removing it may be the repair, and any claim removed with it must be named in your return. That stops at a sentence whose work is to bound what the text asserts — that something is not measured, not claimed, not witnessed or not general, or that the text is an observation of a document rather than a scene from an occasion. Remove or weaken one only where the finding names a defect inside the sentence, and only where a sentence you keep still states that limit in full, so the text bounds what it claims exactly as far as it did, or where the limit contradicts another passage of the same text. Otherwise leave it exactly as it stands and say so. Where the passage carries a claim beside the defect — a fact, an observation, the point the passage exists to make — the smallest change is the one that leaves that claim standing, and deleting the passage entire is not that change. And where you can see no way to remove the defect that does not take the claim with it, leave the passage alone and say so, exactly as you would a finding you cannot repair without inventing a fact: a person can give that claim what it needs or let it go, and a round that deletes it leaves them nothing to weigh. That judgement is about the passage in front of you and never about how much of the text is left — a short text is no licence to leave a finding standing, and a long one is no licence to go on cutting.

A repair at a punctuation joint can be the smallest change even when the finding names the implication created there rather than punctuation itself. In *We finished in March, the finance team got a new reporting tool the same month.*, the defect is the implication created by joining unrelated claims, not either claim. Repair it as *We finished in March. The finance team got a new reporting tool the same month.*: splitting at the joint removes the implication and keeps the reporting-tool fact. Do the same wherever the named defect is confined to a joint; do not delete either side or supply a relationship the text does not establish. This example does not admit a wider mechanics pass: it identifies the smallest repair for the finding already in hand.

Before you return the text, compare it before and after, claim by claim. Every claim you received must still appear with its scope, certainty, attribution, chronology, causality and meaning intact unless the finding named the whole claim as the defect; that exception does not reach a sentence whose work is to bound what the text asserts, which goes only on the two conditions above, and the number or concentration of findings changes nothing about that check. The concentrated anti-slop case makes the boundary visible: removing its patterns must not discard its claims about meeting load, documentation, decisions, satisfaction, distributed work, adoption conditions, or the synchronous/asynchronous trade-off. Repair the patterns around those claims. If one cannot be separated from its pattern, keep it and report the finding unresolved; never compress several content-bearing passages into a cleaner summary.

Where the text is an `article`, a `casestudy`, a `column` or an `opinion`, measure it before you return it: run `uv run "<library>/scripts/article_anatomy.py" -` with the complete corrected text on stdin, under the same `UV_NO_CACHE=1 UV_NO_PROJECT=1` and fresh private `TMPDIR` terms as the resolver above. Exit 0 settles the counted requirements only: it says they hold and nothing about the anatomy requirements the script does not count, so your return reports the text as conforming to the anatomy only where you examined every one of those too, and otherwise names the ones you did not examine. Exit 1 names each counted requirement of the article anatomy that fails, with the part, the rule and the figure measured: repair the ones a finding named and the ones your own repair introduced, then measure again, except a part a finding names as absent and a failure caused only by an absent part, which you leave unwritten and name in your return as left for a person to supply; a requirement the text was already failing when it reached you, and that no finding names, is left exactly as it stands like everything else the findings do not concern. # The base contract

Write with the clarity and factual precision of a well-edited newspaper or quality magazine. Genre, audience, and purpose override that register: a letter, a speech and an advertisement keep their own character. The selected genre governs craft and form; the resolved language governs idiom, syntax and typography. Examples here illustrate meanings, not English phrases to translate.

## Reader and progression

Give the intended reader what they need to understand, judge or do the thing the text is for. Keep a clear focus, introduce unfamiliar concepts before the reasoning needs them, and order material by that reader's needs rather than the writer's discovery process. Relevant technical detail belongs; unexplained jargon and unrelated background do not.

Make the relations between passages real. A transition may explain a connection, but cannot invent one. Keep paragraphs coherent and give supporting material a clear place beside what it supports. The body and its sections remain intelligible without treating a title, standfirst or subheading as their opening sentence.

Open on something specific to the subject. End with what the job calls for: an earned understanding, conclusion, recommendation or next step. Remove introductions and conclusions that add only an announcement or a generic flourish.

## Expression

Use concrete words, useful verbs and a natural, varied cadence. Keep terminology and reference clear; introduce an unfamiliar abbreviation before using it alone. Choose ordinary words where they suffice and established specialist terms where they give this reader precision.

46	
47	Every claim is supported by the text or its material, with exact attribution and proportionate strength. Preserve the state of knowledge: what is unknown or unclaimed is not thereby known not to have happened. Keep uncertainty where it exists and certainty where it is warranted. A fact, quotation, source, scene, personal experience or opinion attributed to somebody is never invented to complete a form. Name the actual source of an attributed claim rather than invoking unnamed studies or experts.

49	Circumstantial detail is a claim too: duration, manner, motive, absence and background all need support. So does an evaluative characterisation: calling a count high, low or modest needs a comparison, target, capacity or speaker assessment. Otherwise give the count with its exclusions, without that assessment.
50	
51	A sequence or correlation establishes no cause. A causal verb such as *shortened* needs causal support; a causal hedge such as *suggests that it shortened* still adds that attribution. This boundary holds in the title, summary, headings and body alike. Preserve chronology, scope and qualifications wherever a claim appears.
52	
53	A stated length constrains the use of material and is never a licence to add to it. When the material is insufficient, deliver the length the material supports and name what further material would close the gap. 54	# Reviewing the base contract
55	
56	Diagnose failures of [the base contract](base.md) in the text in front of you. A finding identifies the passage, the requirement and what the reader loses. Count a loss as the reader who meets the passage in its place would suffer it, not as the strictest reading of a single word could construct it; that holds for every passage, the headline, the standfirst and each subheading as much as the body. A writer's own judgement that the text supports, such as calling a survey small where the text says it reached forty people, is not a claim the text does not carry. Another successful choice, a house-style preference and a mechanical error are not editorial findings; mechanics belongs to the separate final pass. Repetition of whole sentences or passages is an editorial matter, even when the duplication is verbatim; Proofread's duplicate-word correction does not own it.
57	
58	Read for the intended reader's missing step: an unexplained term, a transition asserting a relation the surrounding sentences do not establish, a section whose place obscures the argument. Cover the paratext to find unresolved references in the body. A heading may carry a fact that the section under it does not repeat: a time, a price or a condition a subheading states has been stated to the reader, and is not missing from the body. What is a finding is a body that needs the heading to be understood — a pronoun, a definite form or an ellipsis that only the heading completes — repaired by naming the referent where the body first needs it rather than by saying the heading's facts again. Judge rhythm by its effect, not sentence counts; purposeful repetition, a personal rough edge and a useful digression may be doing essential work.
59	
60	Compare the strength of a claim with the support visible in this text. A number contradicting its stated denominator, a causal conclusion following only a sequence, or a certainty contradicted by a nearby qualification is diagnosable. A plausible quotation or experience is not disproved by the absence of its original source. Review no unseen material, request none, and add no source-verification caveat.
61	
62	Use [the anti-slop catalogue](anti-slop.md) to recognise empty performance, not to prohibit a working figure, contrast or ending. 63	
64	A sentence can do its work by bounding what the text asserts: that something is not measured, not claimed, not witnessed or not general, or that what follows is an observation of a document rather than a scene from an occasion. Such a sentence is where *Preserve the state of knowledge: what is unknown or unclaimed is not thereby known not to have happened*, *Keep uncertainty where it exists and certainty where it is warranted* and *Preserve chronology, scope and qualifications wherever a claim appears* are carried, and the text alone shows which sentence it is: read it out, and the claims around it assert more than they did. That cost is what the removal test above answers, so recognise one by what it bounds and by which claim loses that bound, never by its form. A finding lies inside such a sentence or nowhere: name a limit another sentence already states in full, or a limit contradicting another passage of this text, or leave the sentence exactly as it stands. Naming the whole of it as the defect names nothing inside it.
65	
66	Make the smallest correction that removes a finding. Move or clarify existing material where it supplies the missing connection. Introduce no new evidence, experience, attribution or outcome. If repair would change a claim or a quotation's meaning, or requires information absent from the text, leave the passage and report the unresolved finding. A claim removed because the finding named that claim itself remains part of the claim account, and so does every claim a correction left standing with its scope, certainty, attribution, chronology, causality or meaning moved, and every claim a correction added — one the corrected text asserts and the text before it has no counterpart for, an inference drawn from what that text already said among them where it asserts something that text did not say. A claim that has a counterpart in the text before is changed rather than added. A headline, a standfirst and a subheading carry claims like any other passage, and a changed claim is accounted for by what it now asserts rather than how far its wording moved; a correction that took a limit, a connective or a bounding clause out of the text is accounted for by what the reader no longer has, however little of the text went with it. The account is of the text delivered rather than of the text received, and nothing a reviewing Skill says about the claims as a whole contradicts a finding the same reply states.
67	
68	Compare each correction with its input, including claims beside the defect, then reread the surrounding passage for broken references or transitions. Compare it difference by difference and not by its claims alone, and trace each one to a finding or to what repairing that finding required: a difference answering neither is not a correction, whatever it improves, and the passage it touched belongs back as it was. A correction is a candidate until that comparison and the review after it have run: where the review establishes a defect the correction introduced and its input did not have, the correction is not accepted and its input stands. Preserve functioning wording, voice and formatting outside the finding; concision is not permission to summarise the text away.
69	# General
70	
71	The default genre: the contract a text gets when nobody named a content type. It is a complete contract rather than the absence of one, and it is what a note, a memo, a letter, an explanation, or a piece of prose whose kind has no name is written against.
72	
73	## What this genre asks for
74	
75	**The shape follows the material and the job.** No convention is imposed here — no lede, no summary paragraph, no boilerplate, no mandatory heading, no obligatory recommendation at the end. A named genre brings its reader's expectations with it; this one brings only the reader's need, so the text takes the shape that need implies and no other.
76	
77	**The kind of text is recognisable from the text.** A reader should be able to tell within a sentence or two whether they are holding an explanation, an argument, an account of what happened, a request, or a description, and the text should then behave like that thing throughout. A draft that is an argument for two paragraphs and a chronology for the next two has changed kind without telling anybody.
78	
79	**The register is the baseline's, moved by the audience and the purpose.** With no genre convention to override it, what moves the register is who the text is for and what it is for. A note to a colleague, a public explanation, and a letter of complaint are all this genre, and they are not written the same way. Where the request states or implies an audience or a purpose, that is the instruction; where it does not, hold the baseline.
80	
81	**Length is what the job takes.** There is no expected length here, and nothing is padded to look substantial or cut to look brisk. A text that has done its job in two hundred words is finished at two hundred words.
82	
83	**A title is written when the artifact has one.** Where the requested artifact is a document with a title, the title says what the text is about in the text's own terms, rather than posing a question the text does not answer or promising more than the text delivers. Where the artifact is a passage, a message, or a fragment, no title is invented for it.
84	
85	## What this genre does not do
86	
87	It does not stand in for a genre that exists. Where the request names a content type the Collection installs, that genre's contract is the one to load; this one is what applies when nothing was named and nothing in the request implies a named kind.
88	
89	It adds no requirement the base contract does not already hold. Everything about register, structure, sentences, words, claims, openings, endings, formatting, and consistency is stated there once, and repeating any of it here would make one rule two things to keep true.
90	
91	## The technique this genre is ordinarily written with
92	
93	None. This is the contract a text gets when nobody named a kind of text, and a kind nobody named brings no arc with it. What puts a technique on a text here is a selection, and this genre is not one.
94	# ABT
95	
96	*And, But, Therefore*: Randy Olson's structure connecting a situation and what it puts at stake, a genuine complication or question, and the consequence the material supports. It shapes the reasoning or story without prescribing three paragraphs or visible labels.
97	
98	## What this technique asks for
99	
100	Each part moves from the general to the specific. The And gives the situation, then what is at stake in it: what it makes possible or puts at risk, as the material states it. The But names the complication briefly, then its causes. The Therefore says what follows or is done, then how, where something is done. The general orients every reader; the specific gives the part its force.
101	
102	The reader knows why the situation matters before the complication arrives. A text that opens on its problem leaves the reader asking *so what?* Stakes are facts from the material, never a claim that the subject is important. A calm text often shows them through its situation alone: who has to decide what, and what depends on it. Where the material holds no stakes, state the situation plainly and invent none.
103	
104	The And holds what the complication needs in order to bite and nothing else, and the complication comes early. How much situation that takes depends on what the reader already knows: somebody inside the subject needs little, somebody outside it more.
105	
106	An arc has one complication. Other problems are ordered under it as its causes, not beside it, since two problems of equal rank competing for one consequence leave the reader unsure which to follow. Independent arcs are not that: sections of web copy that each answer their own reader question, a teaser's arc, or a nested or revisited arc.
107	
108	The consequence answers what the complication raised. Each part of it takes up a cause the text has given, so a list of actions is sound when every action answers one; an action against a problem the text never raised is an addition, not a consequence. Where the complication is an open question, or its causes are unknown, the But states it without causes and the consequence takes up the question, for example by naming the next investigation. An open or conditional result is a valid consequence.
109	
110	The relations must hold even without the words *and*, *but* and *therefore*. A step that only adds, this and then that, where a turn or a consequence belongs, is a sequence rather than the relation. A question need not be a crisis, and a response need not be a triumph. For example: a school records room temperatures before deciding whether to change its heating; the readings locate cold periods but do not explain them; the next investigation links readings to room use.
111	
112	Apply the structure at the level the genre's task needs. Where a genre's own rules compress, withhold or reorder part of the arc, as when a teaser withholds its resolution, web copy puts the useful words first or an opinion states its position early, the genre governs. A standfirst or lead may give the result early, open question included; the order above governs where the body develops the arc, not that early answer.
113	
114	Nest or revisit an arc when that helps a complex explanation. In medias res is one possible opening into an event the material actually supplies: the scene itself carries the situation and what is at stake, in the same sentences that move it. It fails when the situation is laid out before the scene, and when it is left out altogether.
115	# The anti-slop catalogue
116	
117	Prose that a language model produced, or that a human wrote after reading a great deal of it, fails in a small number of recognisable ways. This is the catalogue of those ways: what each one looks like on the page, why it costs the reader something, and the smallest change that removes it. It is a diagnostic document — a Skill reading it beside the base contract meets no target the contract does not already hold, and a Skill reading it alone has the patterns and their repairs and needs nothing else.
118	
119	The examples are English because this document is, and they are patterns rather than strings. Apply each by what it does in the target language, and do not look for the English words in it. A word, a phrase, a punctuation convention, or a construction that only exists in one language belongs to that language's own anti-slop guidance instead, where a Skill loads it beside this file.
120	
121	## The test before a pattern is recorded
122	
123	Each pattern below says what a phrase looks like, and looking like one is not being one. Make the repair in your head before you record anything: where the text then asserts more, less or something else than it did, or a distinction it drew is gone, the pattern is not present and nothing is recorded. A hedge that marks genuine doubt, a repetition that lands, a contrast the reader really would otherwise draw wrongly — each of them fails that test, and each is left exactly as it stands.
124	
125	The test comes before the finding rather than after it. A pattern written down reaches whoever repairs it as a defect somebody found, and a guard that only makes the repair careful arrives too late to save the phrase.
126	
127	Repair with the smallest change that removes a pattern the test admits. The writer's vocabulary, their bluntness, their humour, their admitted uncertainty, and their rhythm are what makes a text theirs; a pass that tidies all of it into even prose has replaced one machine voice with another. Leave a strong sentence alone even where it is unusual.
128	
129	## The seven patterns
130	
131	**False contrasts.** A negation used as a run-up to the actual claim: *This isn't a tool. It's a way of working.* *The question isn't whether, but when.* *It's not just faster — it's cheaper.* The rejected half was never in play, so the sentence spends the reader's attention establishing a position nobody held. State the second half on its own: *This changes how the team works.* A contrast stays where the text really is correcting something a reader would otherwise believe.
132	
133	**Empty openings.** A first sentence that announces the subject, asserts that the subject matters, or clears the throat before the text starts: *In today's rapidly changing landscape…*, *Communication has never been more important.*, *Here's the thing.*, *What most people get wrong is…* Each could sit in front of any text at all, which is the test: an opening that would survive being moved to a different article is carrying no information. Cut it and open on the material — a fact, a scene, a tension, the question the text answers. The second paragraph is very often the real opening.
134	
135	**Importance inflation.** Adjectives and formulas that assert weight the material has not shown: *a pivotal moment*, *stands as a testament to*, *a game-changer*, *underscores the significance of*, *plays a vital role in*. Also the trailing participial clause that pretends to interpret — *…, highlighting the team's commitment to quality* — which adds a judgement no fact in the sentence supports. Replace the assertion with what actually happened: *The launch is the company's first paid product.* A reader who is given the fact will decide it matters without being told to.
136	
137	**Vague attribution.** A claim credited to nobody: *Studies show*, *experts agree*, *industry reports suggest*, *it is widely believed*, *many argue*. Nothing here can be checked, and nothing can be contradicted, which is precisely what makes it comfortable to write. Name who found it, who said it, and how they know; where the text has no source, cut the claim rather than dressing it. Do not invent an attribution to satisfy the pattern — an unsourced sentence is removed, never furnished with a plausible source.
138	
139	**Synonym cycling.** One thing given a new name every time it is mentioned, because repeating a word felt like poor style: *the agent* reviews the draft, then *the assistant* scores it, then *the tool* suggests fixes. A reader who has been introduced to three names reasonably assumes three things. Pick the clear name and repeat it. Repetition of a key term is how a reader knows it is the same term, and the fix is usually one word restored in two places rather than a rewritten paragraph. The pattern is present only where the names denote one thing: two words a text uses for two things are not cycling however often they alternate, and a text that named two things comes back naming two things.
140	
141	**Robotic rhythm.** Sentences and paragraphs built to one template: the same length, the same shape, the same three-part list, each paragraph opening with its topic sentence and closing with its summary. # A quiet table on Saturdays

It is Sunday night, the maths homework is due in the morning, and the kitchen table is covered in books, plates and a younger brother's noise. For many families in Pellbrook, that is where homework gets done.

Amira is in year 9. "At home my little brothers are always shouting," she says. Since March she has spent her Saturday mornings somewhere else: the homework club at Pellbrook Library. Her mother drops her off on the way to the market. "Here I get my maths done before lunch."

I repaired finding 1 and left findings 2 and 3 alone, as their notes instruct.

````markdown
# A quiet table on Saturdays

It is Sunday night, the maths homework is due in the morning, and the kitchen table is covered in books, plates and a younger brother's noise. For many families in Pellbrook, that is where homework gets done.

Amira is in year 9. "At home my little brothers are always shouting," she says. Since March she has spent her Saturday mornings somewhere else: the homework club at Pellbrook Library. Her mother drops her off on the way to the market. "Here I get my maths done before lunch."

The club meets every Saturday in term time, from 10:00 to 12:00, in the first-floor study room. It is for pupils in years 7 to 11, it is free, and nobody needs to book: pupils sign in at the door and bring their own homework. There are laptops and a printer, and two volunteer tutors are there each week, one for maths and science and one for English and humanities.

Colin Parry, who tutors maths, is a retired teacher. "Most of them just need someone to ask when they're stuck," he says. On the Saturday we visited, 14 pupils signed in.

So if your Sunday nights look like the one at that kitchen table, the Pellbrook homework club gives your child a quiet table and a volunteer tutor every Saturday, free of charge. Mention it at dinner this week. Saturday morning is when the table is waiting.
````

**Repaired**

- **Finding 1 (the invented scene credited to Amira).** I changed two passages:
  - "For Amira, in year 9, it used to be." now reads "Amira is in year 9."
  - "So if your Sunday nights look like Amira's used to," now reads "So if your Sunday nights look like the one at that kitchen table,"

  **Claim removed:** that the Sunday-night kitchen-table homework used to be Amira's own experience. Finding 1 named that claim as the defect. The material says her brothers shout at home, and nothing about Sunday nights or a kitchen table.

  **Claim changed:** the ending now links the reader's Sunday nights to the opening scene rather than to Amira's past.

  **Still in the text:** her year group, both her quotations, "since March", her mother dropping her off and the "somewhere else" contrast. That contrast now rests on her own "At home" quote.

  **Nothing added:** no new claims, and no limit, connective or bounding clause was removed.

**Left unrepaired**

- **Finding 2 ("For many families in Pellbrook…").** Neither the text nor the material supports the claim. Supporting it would mean inventing a source. The finding says to leave it for the writer, so the sentence is unchanged.
- **Finding 3 (no reason to act now).** The November mock exams and the autumn workload come only from the brief. The brief's requirements are not source evidence, and the finding says not to add them. Left for the writer.

The genre is `general`, so I didn't run the article-anatomy or press-release measurement. I wrote no working files. The language resolver ran in a private `TMPDIR`, which I removed afterwards.
The correction round repaired the one repairable finding and re-review found nothing new. Next is the single mechanical pass through Proofread.

P=$(mktemp -d); echo "$P"; cat > "$P/input.md" <<'EOF'
# A quiet table on Saturdays

It is Sunday night, the maths homework is due in the morning, and the kitchen table is covered in books, plates and a younger brother's noise. For many families in Pellbrook, that is where homework gets done.

Amira is in year 9. "At home my little brothers are always shouting," she says. Since March she has spent her Saturday mornings somewhere else: the homework club at Pellbrook Library. Her mother drops her off on the way to the market. "Here I get my maths done before lunch."

The club meets every Saturday in term time, from 10:00 to 12:00, in the first-floor study room. It is for pupils in years 7 to 11, it is free, and nobody needs to book: pupils sign in at the door and bring their own homework. There are laptops and a printer, and two volunteer tutors are there each week, one for maths and science and one for English and humanities.

Colin Parry, who tutors maths, is a retired teacher. "Most of them just need someone to ask when they're stuck," he says. On the Saturday we visited, 14 pupils signed in.

So if your Sunday nights look like the one at that kitchen table, the Pellbrook homework club gives your child a quiet table and a volunteer tutor every Saturday, free of charge. Mention it at dinner this week. Saturday morning is when the table is waiting.
EOF

# The mechanics contract

Objective correctness, in the half of it that does not depend on which language a text is in. A Skill contracted to mechanical correction reads this document together with the resolved language's own mechanics guidance, and the two together are that run's rules. What is true of every language the Collection installs is stated here and stated once, so that it is not written again in each language, where the copies would be free to disagree with one another about what is an error.

Nothing here is a preference. A rule belongs in this document only where the text is wrong whatever the writer intended, and only where it would be wrong in the same way in any language. Spelling, inflection, agreement, the language's own punctuation, and its conventions for dates, numbers, currency, and quotation all turn on the language and belong to that language's resource. Where a language defaults more strictly or more loosely than a rule below, its own guidance says so, and what it says about itself wins.

The examples are English because this document is, and they are patterns rather than strings. Apply each by what it does in the target language rather than by the words it happens to use.

## Clause boundaries

Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone are an error where the second does not explain, specify, restate, or stand in direct contrast to the first. *The project will be expensive, it starts in the spring* puts two statements in one sentence that have nothing to do with each other beyond sitting there together: the reader takes the comma as a signal that the sentence continues, and meets a new subject and a new verb instead. Two clauses run together with no punctuation at the joint at all are the same error, and take the same correction.

The same joint is not an error where the second clause does explain, specify, restate, or contrast with the first. *The bug was not in the parser, it was in a silent retry* is the negative-positive contrast, where the comma is what holds the two halves together as one statement, and separating them would break a single thought into two. *We shipped it anyway, nobody had a better idea* specifies the first clause with the reason behind it. Both are established usage rather than tolerated looseness, and a pass that corrects them has changed how the sentence reads without being asked to.

Judge a joint by whether the clauses cohere, and not by their length, by how formal the text is, or by how the text punctuates elsewhere. Where the reading is genuinely open — where a careful reader could defend the joint — the comma stands, because what this rule reaches is the boundary that misleads and not the boundary that is merely informal.

Correct an erroneous joint at the joint and nowhere else: the comma becomes a period or a semicolon, and nothing else about the sentence moves. Do not reorder the clauses, do not merge them into one, and do not supply a conjunction — *and*, *but*, and *so* each assert a relation between the two clauses, and the writer asserted none. Neither half is rewritten, split, or tightened on the way past. Where more than one of a period and a semicolon would serve, the period is the safer of the two, since it claims nothing about how closely the statements are related.

## Quotation

Quoted matter reaches a reader in one of three settings, and the setting decides what the punctuation and capitalisation around it have to do. A quotation is run into a sentence, set off as a block of its own, or reported as speech, and a reader takes each of the three as a different promise about where the sentence ends, where the source's words begin, and who is speaking. The marks are the language's. Which glyphs enclose a quotation, which side of a closing mark a stop falls on, and how speech is conventionally set are stated in the resolved language's mechanics scope and not here, and the marks in the examples below stand in for whichever ones it names. What follows holds whatever they turn out to be — which setting a quotation is in, and what that setting then requires.

A run-in quotation is part of the sentence carrying it, and the joint between the two is punctuated by what the quoted words do there. Where the quotation is introduced as an utterance of its own, a stop stands at the joint and the quotation opens the way a sentence opens: *She replied, "I'll be there."* Where the quoted words are instead a grammatical part of the host sentence — its object, its complement, a fragment the sentence reads straight through — no stop stands at the joint and the quotation takes the case the surrounding syntax needs: *She called the proposal "completely unacceptable"*, not *She called the proposal, "Completely unacceptable"*. A stop at that joint promises the reader an utterance and then hands them a sentence with no room for one. Which of a comma and a colon introduces an utterance is a matter for the writer and for the language; whether a stop stands at the joint at all is neither.

The sentence around a run-in quotation still ends, and it ends once. A quoted sentence's own final stop and the host sentence's stop are one stop and not two, and where the quoted matter ends in a question or exclamation mark that mark stands alone and takes no comma beside it: *"Will you?" she asked*, not *"Will you?", she asked*. A reporting clause is bound to the utterance it reports rather than being a sentence in its own right, so it takes no capital and never stands behind a full stop: *"I'll come," she said*, not *"I'll come." She said.* Which side of the closing mark the surviving stop falls on is settled by the language and not here.

A block quotation is marked by being set off, and that setting is the whole of the mark. Marks enclosing a block state the quotation a second time, and they cost the reader the one thing the block was doing for them: inside a block, marks are the source's own and are preserved as the source wrote them. Because the block itself takes no level, a quotation inside one stands at the outermost level the language has rather than at the level it would take nested inside another.

The sentence introducing a block has finished by the time the block begins, and the block ends on the quoted matter's own punctuation, so the surrounding sentence's stop does not follow the block and no part of the host sentence is left hanging past it. A source named with a block sits outside the quotation and after it; set inside, the attribution reads as something the source wrote about itself.

Reported speech is punctuated as a run-in quotation is, and what the setting adds is the layout that says who is speaking. A turn belongs to one speaker and takes a paragraph of its own, and a second speaker beginning inside the first speaker's paragraph is read as the first speaker still talking, however plainly the words belong to somebody else. Where one speaker's turn runs across more than one paragraph, the continuation is marked as the same turn, because a reader shown nothing takes the second paragraph for somebody else's turn: a new paragraph is what a change of speaker looks like in this setting. How a language marks the continuation is its own — a turn left unclosed until its last paragraph, a speech mark opening every one of them — but that the reader can tell one continued turn from two is not the language's to settle.

A quotation promises that the words inside it are the source's, and three departures from that promise are each marked where they occur. Words added or altered so that the quotation fits its host sentence — a pronoun resolved, a tense harmonised, an initial capital raised or lowered to suit the surrounding syntax — are marked as the writer's rather than the source's: *"[T]he proposal was unacceptable"*. Words left out are marked at the gap, so that the reader is not shown a continuous sentence the source never wrote: *"the proposal … was unacceptable"*. An error the source made is kept and marked as the source's — *[sic]* — because quoted matter is not the text's own, and an error corrected inside a quotation makes the quotation false about its source. Unmarked, each of the three reads as the source's own words, which is the single thing the reader took the quotation to guarantee.

## Abbreviations spelled out

The capitals in an abbreviation are a property of the abbreviation and say nothing about the words behind it, so a spelled-out form is capitalised the way those same words are capitalised anywhere else in the text. *Search engine optimisation* and *hypertext markup language* are the forms; *Search Engine Optimisation* and *HyperText Markup Language* are the error, and it comes from reading the capitals backwards out of *SEO* and *HTML*. What it does to a reader is assert a name the text does not have: capitals in running prose mark a proper noun, and a reader meeting them takes the words for the title of a product, a standard, or an organisation rather than for a description of what the abbreviation stands for.

Where the words behind an abbreviation are a proper name, they keep the capitals the name has anyway: *North Atlantic Treaty Organization*, *World Health Organization*. That is the name's capitalisation and not the abbreviation's, which is why the abbreviation is no guide to it — *WHO* and *HTML* look alike, and the words behind them are not the same kind of thing. Correct at the spelled-out form and nowhere else: the abbreviation keeps its own capitals, and where and how the text introduces it is untouched.

## Lists

A list holds one convention for punctuation and capitalisation, and holds it in every item. Which convention it can hold follows from what the items are. Items that are complete sentences are punctuated as sentences, capital and terminal stop, because a sentence does not stop being one for sitting in a list; items that are fragments completing the sentence that introduces them are punctuated as parts of that sentence, and a list of fragments therefore has more than one correct treatment. What is wrong in either case is holding two at once, because the reader takes the change as meaning something: the fragment among sentences reads as truncated, and the one item ending in a stop reads as the end of the list.

Correct at the items that depart from the convention the rest of the list keeps, and nowhere else. The stop closing the last item of a list of fragments is the introducing sentence ending rather than a departure from the list's convention, and it stands. Where the items are genuinely of both kinds, what would have to change is an item and not its punctuation, and rewriting an item is past where a mechanical pass stops.

## Established variants

Where a language establishes more than one correct form, the text's own choice stands. A form is not an error because another form is more common, more modern, or the one the reader would have written, and the correction is never to normalise the text towards one of them. # The mechanics contract

Objective correctness, in the half of it that does not depend on which language a text is in. A Skill contracted to mechanical correction reads this document together with the resolved language's own mechanics guidance, and the two together are that run's rules. What is true of every language the Collection installs is stated here and stated once, so that it is not written again in each language, where the copies would be free to disagree with one another about what is an error.

Nothing here is a preference. A rule belongs in this document only where the text is wrong whatever the writer intended, and only where it would be wrong in the same way in any language. Spelling, inflection, agreement, the language's own punctuation, and its conventions for dates, numbers, currency, and quotation all turn on the language and belong to that language's resource. Where a language defaults more strictly or more loosely than a rule below, its own guidance says so, and what it says about itself wins.

The examples are English because this document is, and they are patterns rather than strings. Apply each by what it does in the target language rather than by the words it happens to use.

## Clause boundaries

Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone are an error where the second does not explain, specify, restate, or stand in direct contrast to the first. *The project will be expensive, it starts in the spring* puts two statements in one sentence that have nothing to do with each other beyond sitting there together: the reader takes the comma as a signal that the sentence continues, and meets a new subject and a new verb instead. Two clauses run together with no punctuation at the joint at all are the same error, and take the same correction.

The same joint is not an error where the second clause does explain, specify, restate, or contrast with the first. *The bug was not in the parser, it was in a silent retry* is the negative-positive contrast, where the comma is what holds the two halves together as one statement, and separating them would break a single thought into two. *We shipped it anyway, nobody had a better idea* specifies the first clause with the reason behind it. Both are established usage rather than tolerated looseness, and a pass that corrects them has changed how the sentence reads without being asked to.

Judge a joint by whether the clauses cohere, and not by their length, by how formal the text is, or by how the text punctuates elsewhere. Where the reading is genuinely open — where a careful reader could defend the joint — the comma stands, because what this rule reaches is the boundary that misleads and not the boundary that is merely informal.

Correct an erroneous joint at the joint and nowhere else: the comma becomes a period or a semicolon, and nothing else about the sentence moves. Do not reorder the clauses, do not merge them into one, and do not supply a conjunction — *and*, *but*, and *so* each assert a relation between the two clauses, and the writer asserted none. Neither half is rewritten, split, or tightened on the way past. Where more than one of a period and a semicolon would serve, the period is the safer of the two, since it claims nothing about how closely the statements are related.

## Quotation

Quoted matter reaches a reader in one of three settings, and the setting decides what the punctuation and capitalisation around it have to do. A quotation is run into a sentence, set off as a block of its own, or reported as speech, and a reader takes each of the three as a different promise about where the sentence ends, where the source's words begin, and who is speaking. The marks are the language's. Which glyphs enclose a quotation, which side of a closing mark a stop falls on, and how speech is conventionally set are stated in the resolved language's mechanics scope and not here, and the marks in the examples below stand in for whichever ones it names. What follows holds whatever they turn out to be — which setting a quotation is in, and what that setting then requires.

A run-in quotation is part of the sentence carrying it, and the joint between the two is punctuated by what the quoted words do there. Where the quotation is introduced as an utterance of its own, a stop stands at the joint and the quotation opens the way a sentence opens: *She replied, "I'll be there."* Where the quoted words are instead a grammatical part of the host sentence — its object, its complement, a fragment the sentence reads straight through — no stop stands at the joint and the quotation takes the case the surrounding syntax needs: *She called the proposal "completely unacceptable"*, not *She called the proposal, "Completely unacceptable"*. A stop at that joint promises the reader an utterance and then hands them a sentence with no room for one. Which of a comma and a colon introduces an utterance is a matter for the writer and for the language; whether a stop stands at the joint at all is neither.

The sentence around a run-in quotation still ends, and it ends once. A quoted sentence's own final stop and the host sentence's stop are one stop and not two, and where the quoted matter ends in a question or exclamation mark that mark stands alone and takes no comma beside it: *"Will you?" she asked*, not *"Will you?", she asked*. A reporting clause is bound to the utterance it reports rather than being a sentence in its own right, so it takes no capital and never stands behind a full stop: *"I'll come," she said*, not *"I'll come." She said.* Which side of the closing mark the surviving stop falls on is settled by the language and not here.

Marks enclosing a block state the quotation a second time, and they cost the reader the one thing the block was doing for them: inside a block, marks are the source's own and are preserved as the source wrote them. Because the block itself takes no level, a quotation inside one stands at the outermost level the language has rather than at the level it would take nested inside another.

The sentence introducing a block has finished by the time the block begins, and the block ends on the quoted matter's own punctuation, so the surrounding sentence's stop does not follow the block and no part of the host sentence is left hanging past it. # A quiet table on Saturdays

It is Sunday night, the maths homework is due in the morning, and the kitchen table is covered in books, plates and a younger brother's noise. For many families in Pellbrook, that is where homework gets done.

Amira is in year 9. "At home my little brothers are always shouting," she says. Since March she has spent her Saturday mornings somewhere else: the homework club at Pellbrook Library. Her mother drops her off on the way to the market. "Here I get my maths done before lunch."

The club meets every Saturday in term time, from 10:00 to 12:00, in the first-floor study room. It is for pupils in years 7 to 11, it is free, and nobody needs to book: pupils sign in at the door and bring their own homework. There are laptops and a printer, and two volunteer tutors are there each week, one for maths and science and one for English and humanities.

Colin Parry, who tutors maths, is a retired teacher. "Most of them just need someone to ask when they're stuck," he says. On the Saturday we visited, 14 pupils signed in.

So if your Sunday nights look like the one at that kitchen table, the Pellbrook homework club gives your child a quiet table and a volunteer tutor every Saturday, free of charge. Mention it at dinner this week. Saturday morning is when the table is waiting.

## The truth of a report about the text

Everything a run says about a text is true of the text it names. That holds for every statement the reply makes about a text, and not only for its findings and its account of the claims: a count, a length, a grammatical label, where a passage stands, and what a round did to a passage — moved it, removed it, replaced it, set a heading over it — each tells the reader something about the text they could check, and each is written so that the check holds.

A statement about the delivered text is checked against the delivered text after the last change to it, the closing mechanical pass included. Most of what a run knows about a text it learned while reviewing the text as it arrived, and the rounds changed that text afterwards, so a length measured before a round or a heading remembered from one describes a text the reader is no longer holding. Where a run measures a text with the Collection Library's measuring script, `scripts/article_anatomy.py`, a count or length the reply states is taken from that script's measurement of the text the statement is about, never from the run's own reading of it and never from a measurement of another state of the text. A statement about the text as it arrived says so, so that nobody reads it against the text delivered. A statement that cannot be made true of the text it names is left out.

The check is made on the reply as drafted, one statement at a time, once the text it describes is final, and each statement is read against the passage it names rather than against what the run remembers of it; a finding written during the review is checked in the same way against the text it was written about. A statement that something holds everywhere or nowhere — that a passage is unchanged, word for word what it was or untouched, that the rest of the text was left alone, that a name appears nowhere else, that a heading says nothing about its section — is checked against every part of the text it covers, because a single exception makes it false, and where there is one the statement names it or is narrowed to what holds. A statement of where wording came from, or of where a passage now stands, is checked by finding that passage in the text.

Who reads it decides this too. The reader of a report finds their way in the text by it, and a statement they check and find false costs them the trust they would have given every other statement in the same reply.
